subject: physics-hl
title: Melting at constant temperature
stem: A pure crystalline solid melts at its melting point while receiving energy. Which microscopic change explains the energy transfer?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B01; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: The average intermolecular potential energy increases.

options.label: B
options.text: The mean random kinetic energy steadily increases.

options.label: D
options.text: The mass of each molecule increases.

steps.text: A. The constant temperature indicates no rise in mean random kinetic energy. Energy changes intermolecular configuration and hence potential energy.

subject: physics-hl
title: Thermal contact
stem: A small hot metal block touches a larger cool block in an insulated box. Which statement about the initial net energy transfer is correct?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B01; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: No energy transfers until their temperatures are equal.

options.label: B
options.text: Energy transfers from the hotter block to the cooler block.

options.label: C
options.text: Energy transfers from the block with greater mass.

options.label: D
options.text: Energy transfers toward the block with greater total internal energy.

steps.text: B. The temperature difference determines the direction of net thermal energy transfer, not mass or total internal energy.

verification.notes: Editorial family B01; physical variant 3/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: B
options.text: The energy needed to lift the sample through one metre.

options.label: C
options.text: The sum of random molecular kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy.

steps.text: C. Internal energy concerns microscopic random kinetic and interaction energies. A stationary sample still has molecular motion.

subject: physics-hl

verification.notes: Editorial family B01; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: The heated air contracts, its density rises, and it rises.

options.label: B
options.text: The molecules become heavier and pull cooler air upward.

options.label: C
options.text: Infrared photons carry the entire air mass upward.

steps.text: D. Heating allows local expansion. Lower-density air experiences a net upward buoyancy force, while cooler air moves in to replace it.

subject: physics-hl
title: Heating through a phase change
stem: A 0.12 kg sample of ice initially at -15 °C is converted completely to water at 12 °C by a heater delivering 150 W to the sample. Take $c_{\mathrm{ice}}$ = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, $c_{\mathrm{water}}$ = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $L_{\mathrm{f}}$ = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. No energy escapes.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B03; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the total energy supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum heating time and explain why temperature stays constant while the ice melts.

steps.text: Separate warming the ice, melting and warming the water: Q = $mc_{\mathrm{ice}}$(0 − $T_{\mathrm{i}}$) + $mL_{\mathrm{f}}$ + $mc_{\mathrm{water}}$ $T_{\mathrm{f}}$.
The contributions are 3.78e+03 J, 4.01e+04 J and 6.05e+03 J, giving Q = 4.99e+04 J.
During melting the supplied energy increases intermolecular potential energy instead of increasing mean random kinetic energy.

subject: physics-hl
title: Heating through a phase change
stem: A 0.3 kg sample of ice initially at 0 °C is converted completely to water at 40 °C by a heater delivering 300 W to the sample. Take $c_{\mathrm{ice}}$ = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, $c_{\mathrm{water}}$ = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $L_{\mathrm{f}}$ = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. No energy escapes.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B03; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the total energy supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum heating time and explain why temperature stays constant while the ice melts.

steps.text: Separate warming the ice, melting and warming the water: Q = $mc_{\mathrm{ice}}$(0 − $T_{\mathrm{i}}$) + $mL_{\mathrm{f}}$ + $mc_{\mathrm{water}}$ $T_{\mathrm{f}}$.
The contributions are 0 J, 1e+05 J and 5.04e+04 J, giving Q = 1.51e+05 J.
During melting the supplied energy increases intermolecular potential energy instead of increasing mean random kinetic energy.

title: A conduction design constraint
stem: A uniform insulating panel has conductivity 0.2 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, area 0.6 m² and thickness 0.025 m. Its faces remain at 60 °C and 10 °C. Edge losses are negligible.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the steady energy-transfer rate through the panel.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The design is changed to reduce this rate by a factor of 2 without changing material, area or face temperatures. Determine the new thickness.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy transferred through the original panel in 2 h.

steps.text: Use the magnitude P = kA($T_{\mathrm{hot}}$ − $T_{\mathrm{cold}}$)/d.
P = 240 W, from the hotter face to the cooler face.
At fixed k, A and temperature difference, P is inversely proportional to d.
$d_{\mathrm{new}}$ = 2d = 0.05 m.

subject: physics-hl
title: Calorimeter data and heat leakage
stem:
The following simulated data describe a 0.25 kg block heated at constant electrical power 30 W. A separate calibration estimates a constant 5 W transfer to the surroundings over this interval. Each temperature reading has uncertainty ±0.10 °C.

| Time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 20.00 |
| 30 | 25.00 |
| 60 | 30.00 |
| 90 | 35.00 |
| 120 | 40.00 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B06; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the full time interval to estimate the rate of temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the specific heat capacity of the block, allowing for the heat leakage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student neglects the heat leakage. State the direction of the resulting error in c and explain it.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest a specific improvement that reduces this bias.

steps.text: Use the difference of endpoint temperatures divided by the 120 s interval.
Gradient = 0.167 K s⁻¹; accept a fit consistent with the displayed readings.
Net power storing thermal energy is $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ = $P_{\mathrm{electrical}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ = mc(dT/dt).
The calculated c is too large: the student attributes all electrical power to raising the block temperature.

subject: physics-hl
title: Calorimeter data and heat leakage
stem:
The following simulated data describe a 0.3 kg block heated at constant electrical power 40 W. A separate calibration estimates a constant 6 W transfer to the surroundings over this interval. Each temperature reading has uncertainty ±0.10 °C.

| Time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 20.00 |
| 30 | 24.25 |
| 60 | 28.50 |
| 90 | 32.75 |
| 120 | 37.00 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B06; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the full time interval to estimate the rate of temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the specific heat capacity of the block, allowing for the heat leakage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student neglects the heat leakage. State the direction of the resulting error in c and explain it.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest a specific improvement that reduces this bias.

steps.text: Use the difference of endpoint temperatures divided by the 120 s interval.
Gradient = 0.142 K s⁻¹; accept a fit consistent with the displayed readings.
Net power storing thermal energy is $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ = $P_{\mathrm{electrical}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ = mc(dT/dt).
The calculated c is too large: the student attributes all electrical power to raising the block temperature.
Add effective thermal insulation around the block, or measure the heat leakage under the same temperature conditions and subtract it.

subject: physics-hl
title: Calorimeter data and heat leakage
stem:
The following simulated data describe a 0.4 kg block heated at constant electrical power 60 W. A separate calibration estimates a constant 8 W transfer to the surroundings over this interval. Each temperature reading has uncertainty ±0.10 °C.

| Time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 20.00 |
| 30 | 23.25 |
| 60 | 26.50 |
| 90 | 29.75 |
| 120 | 33.00 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B06; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the full time interval to estimate the rate of temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the specific heat capacity of the block, allowing for the heat leakage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student neglects the heat leakage. State the direction of the resulting error in c and explain it.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest a specific improvement that reduces this bias.

steps.text: Use the difference of endpoint temperatures divided by the 120 s interval.
Gradient = 0.108 K s⁻¹; accept a fit consistent with the displayed readings.
Net power storing thermal energy is $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ = $P_{\mathrm{electrical}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ = mc(dT/dt).
The calculated c is too large: the student attributes all electrical power to raising the block temperature.
Add effective thermal insulation around the block, or measure the heat leakage under the same temperature conditions and subtract it.

subject: physics-hl
title: Molecular infrared absorption
stem: Why can a greenhouse gas absorb selected infrared frequencies?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B07; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: Its molecular energy-level differences match the photon energies.

options.label: B
options.text: It absorbs every wavelength equally because it is a gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Its molecules must first become electrically charged.

steps.text: A. Absorption is associated with allowed molecular energy changes; photon energy must match an available transition.

subject: physics-hl
title: Re-emission directions
stem: In a simple greenhouse model, an atmospheric layer absorbs infrared radiation from the surface. Which statement about subsequent emission is appropriate?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B07; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: It permanently stores all absorbed radiation.

options.label: B
options.text: It emits infrared in both upward and downward directions.

options.label: D
options.text: It reflects every photon directly back without an energy interaction.

steps.text: B. Thermal emission occurs in all directions, so some emitted radiation returns toward the surface.

subject: physics-hl
title: Natural and enhanced effects
stem: Which change most directly describes an enhanced greenhouse effect?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B07; physical variant 3/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease of all molecular energy levels to zero.

options.label: B
options.text: A greenhouse effect that exists only where glass buildings are present.

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in infrared absorption and emission by greenhouse gases following increased gas concentration.

options.label: D
options.text: The complete removal of sunlight by the atmosphere.

steps.text: C. More greenhouse gas can alter infrared transfer and the radiative balance. The mechanism already exists naturally.

subject: physics-hl
title: A temperature response
stem: A planet initially has balanced incoming and outgoing energy. Outgoing power is then temporarily reduced at unchanged surface temperature. What happens initially?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B07; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: Its stored energy decreases and its temperature falls.

options.label: B
options.text: Its temperature must remain fixed because the original state was balanced.

options.label: D
options.text: Its stored energy increases and its temperature tends to rise.

steps.text: D. Incoming power exceeds outgoing power, giving a positive net energy gain. Warming tends to increase thermal emission.

subject: physics-hl
title: Radiative surface properties
stem: A surface receives 300 W of radiation and scatters 60 W. What is its albedo?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B08; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: A. Albedo = scattered power / incident power = 60/300 = 0.2.

subject: physics-hl
title: Radiative surface properties
stem: A surface receives 400 W of radiation and scatters 120 W. What is its albedo?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B08; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: B. Albedo = scattered power / incident power = 120/400 = 0.3.

subject: physics-hl
title: Radiative surface properties
stem: A surface at 350 K emits 553.06 W m⁻². Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is its emissivity?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B08; physical variant 3/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: C. Emissivity = emitted flux/(σT⁴) = 0.65. It compares the surface with a blackbody at the same temperature.

subject: physics-hl
title: Radiative surface properties
stem: A surface at 420 K emits 1411.5 W m⁻². Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is its emissivity?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B08; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: D. Emissivity = emitted flux/(σT⁴) = 0.8. It compares the surface with a blackbody at the same temperature.

subject: physics-hl
title: Equilibrium-temperature scaling
stem: A simple airless-planet model has equilibrium temperature T. The solar constant doubles while albedo and emissivity stay fixed. What is the new temperature divided by T?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B09; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: A. Balance gives T⁴ proportional to the solar constant. The ratio is $2^{1/4}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Equilibrium-temperature scaling
stem: In an airless-planet model, albedo rises from 0.20 to 0.60. Incoming solar constant and emissivity stay fixed. What is new equilibrium temperature / old equilibrium temperature?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B09; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: B. Absorbed power is proportional to 1 − albedo. Its ratio is 0.40/0.80, so the temperature ratio is $(0.5)^{1/4}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Equilibrium-temperature scaling
stem: In an airless-planet model, emissivity changes from 0.80 to 0.50. Absorbed solar power stays fixed. What is new equilibrium temperature / old equilibrium temperature?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B09; physical variant 3/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: C. At the same absorbed power, emissivity × T⁴ is fixed. The temperature ratio is $(0.80/0.50)^{1/4}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Equilibrium-temperature scaling
stem: Two airless planets have identical albedo and emissivity and orbit the same star. Planet Y is three times as far from the star as planet X. What is $T_{\mathrm{Y}}$/$T_{\mathrm{X}}$ at radiative equilibrium?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B09; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

steps.text: D. Solar flux decreases as distance squared and T is proportional to $\text{flux}^{1/4}$; therefore T is proportional to $\text{distance}^{−1/2}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: A one-layer atmosphere
stem: A spherical planet receives a solar constant of 1200 W m⁻² and has albedo 0.2. In a simplified steady model, the atmosphere transmits all unreflected solar radiation, absorbs all upward surface infrared radiation, and emits the same infrared flux upward and downward. The surface and atmospheric layer emit as blackbodies. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B10; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean absorbed solar flux over the whole planet.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the upward surface infrared flux by balancing the whole planet and then the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the surface temperature and identify one limitation of the model.

steps.text: Average the intercepted sunlight over the full sphere: $F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ = (1 − a)S/4.
$F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ = 240 W m⁻².
Top-of-atmosphere balance requires upward atmospheric emission 240 W m⁻², so downward emission is the same.
Surface balance gives $F_{\mathrm{surface}}$ = $F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ + $F_{\mathrm{down}}$ = 480 W m⁻².
$T = (F_{\mathrm{surface}}/\sigma)^{1/4}$ = 303 K.
A valid limitation is the assumption of complete infrared absorption, no atmospheric solar absorption, a single uniform temperature/layer, or omission of nonradiative heat transfer.

subject: physics-hl
title: A one-layer atmosphere
stem: A spherical planet receives a solar constant of 1360 W m⁻² and has albedo 0.25. In a simplified steady model, the atmosphere transmits all unreflected solar radiation, absorbs all upward surface infrared radiation, and emits the same infrared flux upward and downward. The surface and atmospheric layer emit as blackbodies. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B10; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean absorbed solar flux over the whole planet.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the upward surface infrared flux by balancing the whole planet and then the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the surface temperature and identify one limitation of the model.

steps.text: Average the intercepted sunlight over the full sphere: $F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ = (1 − a)S/4.
$F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ = 255 W m⁻².
Top-of-atmosphere balance requires upward atmospheric emission 255 W m⁻², so downward emission is the same.
Surface balance gives $F_{\mathrm{surface}}$ = $F_{\mathrm{abs}}$ + $F_{\mathrm{down}}$ = 510 W m⁻².
$T = (F_{\mathrm{surface}}/\sigma)^{1/4}$ = 308 K.
A valid limitation is the assumption of complete infrared absorption, no atmospheric solar absorption, a single uniform temperature/layer, or omission of nonradiative heat transfer.

stem: An airless spherical body has solar constant 1000 W m⁻², albedo 0.15 and emissivity 0.9. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. Assume its surface has one uniform temperature.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for its equilibrium temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the original temperature and the new temperature if albedo rises to 0.19 with everything else fixed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why using a single global temperature can be a limitation even if total incoming power is known.

steps.text: Set absorbed power (1 − a)Sπr² equal to emitted power eσT⁴(4πr²).
Cancel πr² and rearrange: $T = [(1 − a)S/(4eσ)]^{1/4}$.
$T_{\mathrm{original}}$ = 254 K; $T_{\mathrm{new}}$ = 251 K.
Real surfaces can have day/night and latitude temperature differences.
Emission depends on the fourth power of local temperature, so emission computed at an average temperature need not equal the actual average emission.

subject: physics-hl
title: Auditing a satellite radiation budget
stem: A simulated satellite dataset gives global mean fluxes for a planet: incoming solar 300 ± 3 W m⁻², reflected solar 66 ± 3 W m⁻², and outgoing thermal 234 ± 3 W m⁻². Each quoted uncertainty is an absolute maximum uncertainty. Treat the mean budget as steady.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B12; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the planetary albedo.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the net retained flux and its maximum absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the effective blackbody temperature corresponding to the outgoing thermal flux, using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A proposed model predicts a retained flux of 6 W m⁻². Is it distinguishable from zero using these quoted uncertainty bounds?

steps.text: a = reflected/incoming = 66/300 = 0.22.
$F_{\mathrm{net}}$ = incoming − reflected − outgoing = 0 W m⁻².
For this sum/difference, add absolute uncertainties: $\Delta F_{\mathrm{net}}$ = 9 W m⁻².
$T_{\mathrm{eff}} = (F_{\mathrm{out}}/\sigma)^{1/4}$ = 253 K.
No. 6 W m⁻² lies inside the measurement interval ±9 W m⁻², so these measurements do not resolve the proposed imbalance.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B17; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the rms molecular speed.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the density and hence the pressure using the kinetic model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the total internal energy and explain why the container can be stationary while this energy is nonzero.

steps.text: Equate ½m $v_{\mathrm{rms}}$² to $3k_{\mathrm{B}}$ T/2, giving $v_{\mathrm{rms}}$ = sqrt($3k_{\mathrm{B}}$ T/m).
$v_{\mathrm{rms}}$ = 1.37e+03 m s⁻¹.
ρ = Nm/V = 0.0443 kg m⁻³.
P = $\rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}$²/3 = 2.76e+04 Pa.
U = $3Nk_{\mathrm{B}}$ T/2 = 124 J.
The energy belongs to random particle motion; zero centre-of-mass velocity does not mean zero molecular velocities.

subject: physics-hl
title: Testing an isothermal gas model
stem:
A simulated compression experiment holds a fixed gas sample at 300 K. The readings below use absolute pressure. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

| Volume / cm³ | Absolute pressure / kPa |
|---:|---:|
| 20 | 3116.25 |
| 25 | 2493.00 |
| 30 | 2077.50 |
| 40 | 1558.13 |
| 50 | 1246.50 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B18; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate PV for the smallest and largest volumes and assess the isothermal ideal-gas prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the mean PV product to estimate the amount of gas.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State what should be plotted to obtain a straight line through the origin and identify its gradient.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why compressing quickly could invalidate this test.

steps.text: The endpoint products are 62325 and 62325 kPa cm³.
They agree to the displayed precision, consistent with constant PV for fixed amount and temperature. This supports the model but does not prove it.
Convert 1 kPa cm³ = 10⁻³ J, then use n = mean(PV)/(RT).
Plot absolute pressure P against 1/V; the gradient is nRT when SI units are used.
Rapid compression can raise the gas temperature before it exchanges heat with the surroundings, so the fixed-temperature assumption fails.

options.label: A
options.text: A spontaneous process with a positive total entropy change.

options.label: B
options.text: A spontaneous process with a negative total entropy change.

options.label: C
options.text: A refrigerator lowering total entropy without any other change.

options.label: D
options.text: Heat flowing spontaneously from cold to hot with no compensating effect.

steps.text: A. An irreversible spontaneous process increases the entropy of an isolated system; the reversible limit has zero change.

subject: physics-hl
title: Local entropy decrease
stem: A refrigerator lowers the entropy of its contents. Which condition is required for consistency with the second law?

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B20; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

options.label: A
options.text: The contents must be an isolated system.

options.label: B
options.text: The entropy increase of the surroundings is at least as large.

options.label: C
options.text: The surroundings must also lose entropy.

options.label: D
options.text: The work input must be zero.

steps.text: B. The contents are not isolated. Their entropy reduction is compensated by heat rejection and work-related dissipation in the surroundings.

steps.text: C. Entropy is a state function. At the end of a complete cycle the gas returns to its initial state, so its entropy change is zero.

subject: physics-hl
title: A directional gas cycle
stem: A fixed amount of gas follows the rectangular cycle shown, returning to its initial state. The arrows give the direction. The pressure limits are 80 kPa and 200 kPa; the volume limits are 1 × 10⁻³ m³ and 4 × 10⁻³ m³. Use the convention that work done by the gas is positive.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done by the gas in one cycle.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the net heat transferred into the gas per cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain whether the cycle produces net mechanical work or requires net mechanical input.

steps.text: The magnitude is the enclosed area: ($P_{\mathrm{high}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{low}}$)($V_{\mathrm{high}}$ − $V_{\mathrm{low}}$).
The cycle is clockwise, so W = +360 J. The kPa × 10⁻³ m³ factors give joules.
The gas returns to the same state, so $\Delta U_{\mathrm{cycle}}$ = 0.
$Q_{\mathrm{net}}$ = ΔU + W = +360 J.
It produces net mechanical work because W is positive.

title: A directional gas cycle
stem: A fixed amount of gas follows the rectangular cycle shown, returning to its initial state. The arrows give the direction. The pressure limits are 100 kPa and 230 kPa; the volume limits are 2 × 10⁻³ m³ and 6 × 10⁻³ m³. Use the convention that work done by the gas is positive.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B21; physical variant 2/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done by the gas in one cycle.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the net heat transferred into the gas per cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain whether the cycle produces net mechanical work or requires net mechanical input.

steps.text: The magnitude is the enclosed area: ($P_{\mathrm{high}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{low}}$)($V_{\mathrm{high}}$ − $V_{\mathrm{low}}$).
The cycle is anticlockwise, so W = -520 J. The kPa × 10⁻³ m³ factors give joules.
The gas returns to the same state, so $\Delta U_{\mathrm{cycle}}$ = 0.
$Q_{\mathrm{net}}$ = ΔU + W = -520 J.
It requires net mechanical input because W is negative.

title: A monatomic adiabatic change
stem: A fixed 0.2 mol sample of monatomic ideal gas initially has temperature 420 K and volume 0.00500 m³. It changes adiabatically to volume 0.01 m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $PV^{5/3}$ = constant.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B22; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the final temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in internal energy and work done by the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the sign of the temperature change using energy transfer.

steps.text: Combine $PV^{5/3}$ = constant with PV = nRT to obtain $TV^{2/3}$ = constant.
ΔU = 3nR($T_{\mathrm{f}}$ − $T_{\mathrm{i}}$)/2 = -387 J.
Q = 0, so W = −ΔU = 387 J.
During expansion the gas does work with no heat input, reducing its internal energy and temperature.

subject: physics-hl
title: Testing an engine claim
stem: A steady heat engine absorbs 4e+04 W from a reservoir at 600 K and produces useful mechanical power 9.6e+03 W. It rejects its remaining heat to a reservoir at 300 K.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B23; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate its actual efficiency and the Carnot efficiency for these reservoirs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the heat-rejection rate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the total entropy increase of the reservoirs each second and use it to assess whether the stated engine violates the second law.

steps.text: $\eta_{\mathrm{actual}}$ = $P_{\mathrm{useful}}$/$P_{\mathrm{in}}$ = 0.24 (24%).
$\eta_{\mathrm{Carnot}}$ = 1 − $T_{\mathrm{c}}$/$T_{\mathrm{h}}$ = 0.5 (50%).
$P_{\mathrm{rejected}}$ = $P_{\mathrm{in}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{useful}}$ = 3.04e+04 W.
Entropy rate = $P_{\mathrm{rejected}}$/$T_{\mathrm{c}}$ − $P_{\mathrm{in}}$/$T_{\mathrm{h}}$ = 34.7 J K⁻¹ s⁻¹.
The total entropy rate is positive and the efficiency is below the reversible limit, so these figures do not violate the second law.

subject: physics-hl
title: Two descriptions of entropy
stem: Two ideal thermal reservoirs exchange 120 J. Their fixed temperatures are 400 K and 280 K. Separately, a simple model has 4 accessible equally probable microstates before a constraint is removed and 8 afterward. Use $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B24; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For heat flowing from the hotter reservoir to the colder one, calculate the entropy change of each reservoir and the combined change.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why reversing this transfer without another change is not spontaneous.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the entropy change of the microstate model.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why a macrostate with more equally probable microstates is more likely.

steps.text: $\Delta S_{\mathrm{hot}}$ = −Q/$T_{\mathrm{h}}$ = -0.3 J K⁻¹; $\Delta S_{\mathrm{cold}}$ = Q/$T_{\mathrm{c}}$ = 0.429 J K⁻¹.
$\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}}$ = 0.129 J K⁻¹.
Reversal would make the combined entropy change negative, contradicting the second law for the isolated pair.
ΔS = $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ ln $\Omega_{\mathrm{f}}$ − $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ ln $\Omega_{\mathrm{i}}$ = $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ ln($\Omega_{\mathrm{f}}$/$\Omega_{\mathrm{i}}$).
There are more distinct microscopic arrangements corresponding to that macrostate, so its total probability is larger.

answerSummary: Reservoir total 0.129 J K⁻¹; microstate change 9.57e-24 J K⁻¹

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script

options.label: A
options.text: It adds its resistance in series with the cell.

options.label: B
options.text: It guarantees zero current through the divider.

options.label: C
options.text: It increases that branch resistance to infinity.

options.label: D
options.text: It provides a parallel path and lowers that branch resistance.

steps.text: D. The finite meter is in parallel with the resistor, so their combined resistance is smaller. This loading can alter the measured potential difference.

title: A source under load
stem: A cell has emf 6 V and constant internal resistance 0.4 Ω. It supplies a single external resistor of 3 Ω. Connecting wires have negligible resistance.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B27; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and the terminal potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the power transferred inside the cell and the fraction of its electrical power delivered to the external resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why terminal voltage rises when the external resistance is increased.

steps.text: I = ε/(R + r).
I = 1.76 A; terminal V = IR = 5.29 V.
$P_{\mathrm{internal}}$ = I²r = 1.25 W.
Fraction = I²R/(εI) = R/(R+r) = 0.882.
Larger external resistance reduces the current, so the internal drop Ir decreases and V = ε − Ir rises.

title: A sensor-divider threshold
stem: An ideal 6 V supply feeds a series combination of a 2000 Ω fixed resistor and an LDR. The LDR initially has resistance 6000 Ω. The output is measured from the midpoint to the lower node by an ideal voltmeter. The diagram shows which resistor is above the midpoint.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B28; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial output potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Brighter light halves the LDR resistance. Calculate the new output potential difference.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the direction of the output change in terms of the resistance ratio.

steps.text: For the lower resistor, $V_{\mathrm{out}}$ = $\varepsilon R_{\mathrm{lower}}$/($R_{\mathrm{upper}}$ + $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$).
$V_{\mathrm{out}}$ = 4.5 V.
Use $R_{\mathrm{LDR,new}}$ = 3e+03 Ω in the divider expression.
$V_{\mathrm{out,new}}$ = 3.6 V.
The LDR is below the midpoint. Reducing its resistance reduces its fraction of total resistance, so output falls.

title: A sensor-divider threshold
stem: An ideal 12 V supply feeds a series combination of a 5000 Ω fixed resistor and an LDR. The LDR initially has resistance 3000 Ω. The output is measured from the midpoint to the lower node by an ideal voltmeter. The diagram shows which resistor is above the midpoint.

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B28; physical variant 4/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial output potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Brighter light halves the LDR resistance. Calculate the new output potential difference.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the direction of the output change in terms of the resistance ratio.

steps.text: For the lower resistor, $V_{\mathrm{out}}$ = $\varepsilon R_{\mathrm{lower}}$/($R_{\mathrm{upper}}$ + $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$).
$V_{\mathrm{out}}$ = 7.5 V.
Use $R_{\mathrm{LDR,new}}$ = 1.5e+03 Ω in the divider expression.
$V_{\mathrm{out,new}}$ = 9.23 V.
The fixed resistor is below the midpoint. Reducing the upper LDR resistance increases the lower resistor’s fraction of total resistance, so output rises.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total charge passing a cross-section and the electrical energy transferred.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The same material and length are used with twice the diameter. State the factor change in power for the same ideal voltage supply.

steps.text: Use cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² and R = ρL/A; convert diameter to metres.
Area increases by four and resistance falls to one quarter. Since P = V²/R at fixed voltage, power increases by a factor of four.

subject: physics-hl
title: Separating wire and contact resistance
stem:
A simulated investigation uses uniform wire of measured diameter 0.4 ± 0.010 mm. The measured resistance includes the wire and an approximately constant contact resistance. The model is $R_{\mathrm{measured}}$ = (ρ/A)L + $R_{\mathrm{contact}}$.

| Wire length / m | Measured resistance / Ω |
|---:|---:|
| 0.20 | 0.80 |
| 0.40 | 1.40 |
| 0.60 | 2.00 |
| 0.80 | 2.60 |
| 1.00 | 3.20 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B30; physical variant 1/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the gradient and intercept of resistance against length, with units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the wire resistivity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Ignoring uncertainty in the gradient, estimate the percentage uncertainty in the resistivity due to the diameter measurement.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why calculating $R_{\mathrm{measured}}$ A/L separately for each length produces a length-dependent apparent resistivity.

steps.text: Gradient = ΔR/ΔL = 3 Ω m⁻¹.
Intercept = 0.2 Ω, interpreted as contact resistance.
ρ = gradient × A, with A = πd²/4.
Because ρ is proportional to d², percentage uncertainty = 2Δd/d × 100 = 5%.
The contact resistance contributes an extra term $R_{\mathrm{contact}}$ A/L. Its effect is larger at short lengths, so that calculation cannot isolate the material resistivity.

subject: physics-hl
title: Separating wire and contact resistance
stem:
A simulated investigation uses uniform wire of measured diameter 0.5 ± 0.010 mm. The measured resistance includes the wire and an approximately constant contact resistance. The model is $R_{\mathrm{measured}}$ = (ρ/A)L + $R_{\mathrm{contact}}$.

| Wire length / m | Measured resistance / Ω |
|---:|---:|
| 0.20 | 1.40 |
| 0.40 | 2.40 |
| 0.60 | 3.40 |
| 0.80 | 4.40 |
| 1.00 | 5.40 |

verification.method: Deterministic calculation and model/units checks in the independent authoring script
verification.notes: Editorial family B30; physical variant 3/4. Original stem, values and diagrams. Author checked signs, units, givens and mark totals; independent editorial review is separate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the gradient and intercept of resistance against length, with units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the wire resistivity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Ignoring uncertainty in the gradient, estimate the percentage uncertainty in the resistivity due to the diameter measurement.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why calculating $R_{\mathrm{measured}}$ A/L separately for each length produces a length-dependent apparent resistivity.

steps.text: Gradient = ΔR/ΔL = 5 Ω m⁻¹.
Intercept = 0.4 Ω, interpreted as contact resistance.
ρ = gradient × A, with A = πd²/4.
Because ρ is proportional to d², percentage uncertainty = 2Δd/d × 100 = 4%.
The contact resistance contributes an extra term $R_{\mathrm{contact}}$ A/L. Its effect is larger at short lengths, so that calculation cannot isolate the material resistivity.

subject: physics-hl
title: Heating and melting with a measured heat loss
stem:
A heater supplies constant electrical power $80\,\mathrm{W}$ to a $0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ sample. Independent measurements show constant heat loss $10\,\mathrm{W}$. In simulated observations, the sample warms by $40\,\mathrm{K}$ in $102.857143\,\mathrm{s}$, then melts at constant temperature for $120\,\mathrm{s}$. Neglect the container heat capacity.

Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the rate of thermal energy increase of the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the specific heat capacity before melting.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the specific latent heat of fusion.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why temperature remains constant during melting.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: State how ignoring heat loss would affect the calculated specific heat capacity.

steps.text: Subtract heat loss from electrical input power.
$mc\Delta T=(P-P_\mathrm{loss})t$.
$mL=(P-P_\mathrm{loss})t_\mathrm{melt}$.
Energy increases the intermolecular potential energy as structure changes.
It does not increase the mean kinetic energy associated with temperature during the phase change.
It would overestimate the thermal energy absorbed and hence overestimate the specific heat capacity.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Displayed six-decimal warming time substituted in Q=mcΔT gives900within displayed precision; latentheat=42000.0; positive constant losses accounted for both stages.

subject: physics-hl
title: A planet in a simple radiation-balance model
stem:
A spherical planet of radius $5.00\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ receives stellar intensity $1100\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ on a surface perpendicular to the incoming rays. Its albedo is $0.20$ and emissivity is $0.90$. It has a uniform temperature, no internal heating and no atmosphere. Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-4}}$.

Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the different areas used for interception and thermal emission.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the absorbed stellar power.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the equilibrium temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The albedo increases to $0.30$ while all other model inputs stay unchanged. Calculate the new temperature.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain one limitation when applying this model to a real planet.

steps.text: The projected disc intercepts radiation over area $\pi R^2$.
The entire spherical surface emits over area $4\pi R^2$.
$P_\mathrm{abs}=(1-\alpha)S\pi R^2$.
Balance absorbed power with $4\pi R^2\epsilon\sigma T^4$.
$T=256\,\mathrm{K}$.
Use the same balance, or $T_2/T_1=[(1-\alpha_2)/(1-\alpha_1)]^{1/4}$.
A real atmosphere can absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, or nonuniform temperatures can change the emitted power; accept one explained limitation.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Absorbed and emitted powers balance at256.24138799301437K; radius cancels from uniform equilibrium; changed albedo gives247.8285245874132K. No unsupported atmosphere trapping model.

subject: physics-hl
title: An isothermal helium sample
stem:
A sealed sample of helium is modelled as a monatomic ideal gas at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. The following pressure-volume readings are simulated. Use $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ and molar mass $M=0.00400\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}$.

| $V$ / L | $p$ / kPa |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 199.44 |
| 2 | 99.72 |
| 3 | 66.48 |
| 4 | 49.86 |



Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the first reading to determine the amount of gas in moles.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how all four readings support an isothermal ideal-gas model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square molecular speed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the internal energy of the sample.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: State conditions under which the ideal-gas approximation is most reliable.

steps.text: Convert kPa to Pa and litres to $\mathrm{m^3}$ in $pV=nRT$.
$n=0.0800\,\mathrm{mol}$.
The product of absolute pressure and volume is constant within the displayed rounding.
For fixed gas amount, the ideal-gas equation therefore gives constant absolute temperature.
$v_\mathrm{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}$.
For the stated monatomic ideal gas, $U=\frac32nRT$.
$U=299\,\mathrm{J}$.
Low density or low pressure and a temperature sufficiently far from condensation, so intermolecular forces and molecular volume are negligible.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Pressure in kPa times volume in L has unitsJ; amount from first displayedrow=0.08; allpVvaluesagree; rms speed=1367.3880210093987; monatomic internalenergy=299.15999999999997.

title: Terminal voltage and an internal resistance
stem:
A cell gives the following simulated terminal potential differences at different steady currents. Assume constant emf and internal resistance.

| $I$ / A | $V$ / V |
| --- | --- |
| 0.1 | 1.46 |
| 0.2 | 1.42 |
| 0.3 | 1.38 |
| 0.4 | 1.34 |



Give calculated numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the emf and internal resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: At $I=0.300\,\mathrm{A}$ calculate the load resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At that current find useful load power and internal heating power.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain the intercept obtained when current tends to zero.

steps.text: Use $V=\mathcal E-rI$; the gradient is $-r$ and intercept is $\mathcal E$.
$\mathcal E=1.50\,\mathrm{V}$.
$R_\mathrm{load}=V/I$, using terminal rather than emf voltage.
$R_\mathrm{load}=4.60\,\Omega$.
Use $P_\mathrm{load}=IV$ and $P_\mathrm{internal}=I^2r$.
$P_\mathrm{load}=0.414\,\mathrm{W}$; $P_\mathrm{internal}=0.0360\,\mathrm{W}$.
There is negligible internal voltage drop, so terminal voltage tends to the emf.

verification.method: Author numerical, dimensional and model-consistency checks; independent review recorded separately
verification.notes: Endpoint slope exactly−0.4; intercept1.5; at0.300A loadR=4.6,loadP=0.414,internalP=0.036; load plus internal power equals emf times current.

parts.prompt: Explain the intercept obtained when current tends to zero.

steps.text: Use $V=\mathcal E-rI$; the gradient is $-r$ and intercept is $\mathcal E$.

$R_\mathrm{load}=5.30\,\Omega$.
Use $P_\mathrm{load}=IV$ and $P_\mathrm{internal}=I^2r$.
$P_\mathrm{load}=0.477\,\mathrm{W}$; $P_\mathrm{internal}=0.0630\,\mathrm{W}$.
There is negligible internal voltage drop, so terminal voltage tends to the emf.
